title: Silver roofs
hookLine: if not for people all becoming one in disbelief, the deniers would have had silver roofs, and it's all the enjoyment of this life (43:33–35)

cards: 'Umar walks into a small room in Medina and finds the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ lying on a rough mat of palm fiber, with nothing between it and his skin. When he sits up, the weave has left lines pressed into his side.

A leather pillow stuffed with fiber. A little barley in the corner. 'Umar looks around and starts to cry. He's thinking of the kings of Persia and Rome in their palaces, and here is the Messenger of Allah on a mat.
The Prophet asks him why he's crying. His answer, in Bukhari, is close to today's verses.

teach.b: Surah Az-Zukhruf, verses thirty-three to thirty-five.

The surah is pushing back on a claim it quotes a few verses earlier: if this message were true, wouldn't it have come to some great man of the two cities, someone rich? So the Qur'an answers with an image.

If it weren't that all people would become one community of deniers, chasing it, Allah would have given those who deny the Most Merciful roofs of silver for their houses, and silver stairways to climb, and doors, and couches to lean on, and zukhruf, gold ornament.
Then the verdict: all of that is only the enjoyment of the life of this world, and the hereafter with your Lord is for the mindful.
Commentators draw out the point: in this picture, silver roofs are so slight a thing they could be handed to people who reject Him, except that everyone would then chase the silver.
Wealth isn't a sign of being favored, and it isn't the scale anyone is weighed on.
Zukhruf, the surah's name, means gold, the ornament laid over a surface: beautiful, and on the outside. Back to 'Umar in the little room.

teach.h: THEY HAVE THIS WORLD; WE, THE NEXT.
teach.b: The Prophet answered him: wouldn't you be content that they have this world, and we have the hereafter? Not a rule against owning things; the companions included merchants and the wealthy.
A rule about where the weight goes. And a hadith in al-Tirmidhi says it more sharply: if this world were worth a mosquito's wing to Allah, He wouldn't give a denier a sip of water from it.

how: Muslim teaching on zuhd, detachment from worldly things, often cites Az-Zukhruf 33–35 and the Prophet's simple room; many Muslims understand wealth as a trust to be used well, not a sign of God's favor.

o: the gilded domes of the first great mosques
the riches of this world, slight next to the hereafter
the fine houses the companions built in Medina

p: only the enjoyment of this life

s: the Qur'an says wealth is a sign of Allah's favor
43:33–35 says silver roofs are so cheap He'd give them to deniers.
the Prophet's room had a rough palm-fiber mat that marked his skin
'Umar saw the lines and wept, as Bukhari reports.
the companions were forbidden to own anything
some were merchants and wealthy; the teaching is about where the weight goes.

games.q: you're 'Umar, crying at the Prophet's mat while kings live in palaces. what does the Prophet say?
o: wouldn't you be content that they have this world, and we the hereafter?
don't cry; it's only a mat.
games.why: wouldn't you be content that they have this world, and we have the hereafter? the weight goes on what lasts.

practice: Let something come to mind that you've wanted lately: a phone, a kitchen, a car, a look, and see it clearly, without judging the wanting.
Now picture it a few years from now, scratched, out of date, replaced, and notice which part of you still wants it. Then let it rest, lightly, like gold leaf.

wordCard.voice: Silver roofs. Az-Zukhruf's picture: silver roofs and gold ornament, so cheap to Allah He'd give them to deniers, all only the enjoyment of this life. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: gold ornament, gilding, the name of surah forty-three.

carryVoice: Your line: ornaments pass. Gold is beautiful, and on the outside. Day five hundred seventy, done.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4913; Sahih Muslim 1479 ('Umar and the mat)
